Kirttan Shah on Instagram: "If you are still clueless on the bloodbath in the global stock markets watch this 2 minute video for the entire summary. The answer is the AI bubble, Let me explain, 

The back bone of AI is compute, so when you ask a question it can reply quickly, for which you need chips for processing the data, memory to store data and to package all of this you need a data centre or like you also call it a hyperscaler. 

When AI started, companies like oracle, alphabet etc used money from their balance sheet to buy these chips & memory to build the Hyperscalers. Then they realised that this requires massive investments. So they started taking debt from the market. Some even sold some shares to raise funds for it.

Then came a better option called neo clouds. These are companies which act like banks. So neo clouds like core weave etc started raising debt from the market to build compute and charge a rent to who ever wants to use the compute & not invest their own money to build the Hyperscalers 

Today there are 200+ of these neo clouds renting compute to big tech but are now not able to raise more money to finish existing Hyperscalers & spend money to build the new ones as planned.

If Hyperscalers don’t get built then less compute and if less compute, AI can’t scale. Markets have been sensing this for a while and hence Korea, Taiwan, Japan, China etc index and stocks have been massively falling for sometime now. 

What changed yesterday was the market realisation that after trump lost the mid term election and with democrats in the congress, it’s not going to be as easy for the AI spending’s to continue as it was happening so far and hence the bloodbath in US. While you might have seen the market fall only yesterday but most AI stocks are already down 50-60% in the US.

The bubble bursted a long time back, you just noticed it yesterday! 

#aibubble #aibubbleburst #nasdaq #midtermelections #trump"

It literally translates to: ”After eating you should rest, or walk a thousand steps."

I would definitely go for walking a thousand steps.

Some more hacks to help reduce the spike:

•⁠ ⁠Have a veggie starter before your pasta - a green salad, roasted asparagus or some baby carrots will do the trick. The fiber in veggies will help form a protective mesh slowing down how quickly glucose from the pasta arrives.
•⁠ ⁠Add some vinegar - try having 1 tbsp of apple cider vinegar in a large glass of water before your meal (preferably with a straw to protect your teeth). The acetic acid in vinegar can help reduce the glucose spike after eating.
•⁠ ⁠Put some clothes on your pasta - add chicken, olive oil or parmesan. The protein and fat help slow down digestion and how quickly glucose enters your bloodstream.

Idris | Online Fitness Coach on Instagram: "How to Properly Perform the Standing Single-Arm Dumbbell Shoulder Press
Target Muscles: Deltoids (Anterior & Medial), Triceps
Equipment: Dumbbell
Difficulty Level: Intermediate
▶ STARTING POSITION
1. Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart.
2. Brace your core (abs and midsection) and maintain a neutral spine.
3. Hold the dumbbell at shoulder level (between your chin and collarbone).
4. Keep your elbow slightly in front of your body, aligned with the scapular plane (at about a 30 to 45-degree angle).
5. Keep your shoulders down and back (avoid shrugging).
6. Stack your wrist directly over your elbow.
7. Keep a slight bend in your knees for stability and balance.
▶ PRESSING PHASE
1. Press the dumbbell overhead in a controlled manner until your arm is fully extended.
2. Avoid aggressively locking out your elbow at the top.
3. Keep your ribs down and avoid overarching your lower back.
4. Keep your torso stable; do not lean backward or tilt to the side.
5. Exhale as you press the weight up.
6. Keep the movement smooth and controlled.
▶ LOWERING PHASE
1. Slowly lower the dumbbell back to shoulder level.
2. Maintain scapular control and don’t let your shoulder roll forward.
3. Keep your elbow slightly in front of your torso throughout the descent.
4. Inhale as you lower the weight back down.
5. Keep your core engaged throughout the entire movement.

Tim Spector MSC FRCP MD FRSB OBE on Instagram: "Cold and flu season is here, and there are a few simple things I do at the first sign of a cold to help ease the symptoms and hopefully shorten its duration.

At the first tickle of a sore throat or blocked nose, I reach for a saline nasal spray. There’s some encouraging evidence that using one early can help reduce how long a cold lasts.

I also focus on eating plenty of plants. Kiwis, peppers and broccoli are excellent sources of vitamin C, alongside fibre and polyphenols that help support our overall health. Vitamin C supplements are unlikely to make much difference once a cold has started.

It’s tempting to reach for sugary snacks and refined carbohydrates when you’re feeling miserable, but I try to stick to nourishing meals with plenty of plants. I also keep eating fermented foods like kimchi, kefir and miso to support my gut microbes, which play an important role in regulating our immune system.

If I’m particularly congested, a saltwater nasal rinse can help clear mucus and make breathing easier. Just make sure you use sterile, distilled or previously boiled and cooled water.

And don’t underestimate the basics. Get plenty of rest, stay hydrated and give yourself time to recover. I find a warm drink particularly comforting when I have a sore throat, often a fermented lemon and ginger drink from aguamadre with hot water and honey. This is not an ad, I just really love their products.

These are some of the habits I rely on when a cold strikes. They won’t prevent every infection, but a few small steps can make those miserable days a little more manageable. I hope this helps!

Dr. Rhonda Patrick on Instagram: "Can supplements slow cognitive decline? I think a few show promise:

Omega-3s (EPA and DHA) - Important for neuronal membranes, brain function, and resolving inflammation. Higher omega-3 levels are associated with lower dementia risk.

Multivitamins - Daily multivitamins improved cognition in older adults in the COSMOS trials, with benefits equivalent to roughly 2 fewer years of global cognitive aging.

Vitamin D - Supplementation has been associated with a 40% lower dementia risk, while low vitamin D levels are linked to a 50 to 80% higher risk.

Creatine - 20 g/day for 8 weeks increased brain creatine by 11% and improved several cognitive measures in a small Alzheimer’s pilot study. This one is promising, but preliminary.

Sulforaphane - Increases glutathione levels in the brain. Early trials also suggest cognitive benefits.

Exogenous ketones - Provide an alternative fuel for the brain, potentially compensating for impaired glucose metabolism in people with cognitive impairment.

None of these is proven to prevent dementia, but they represent promising approaches to supporting brain health through nutrition, energy metabolism, and inflammation regulation.

And remember, supplements should complement (not replace) the fundamentals like exercise, sleep, and metabolic health!"
